definition: Yarn count is a number expressing a yarn's fineness as length per unit mass (indirect systems such as Ne and Nm) or mass per unit length (direct systems such as tex and denier).
explanation: Two families of count coexist. Indirect systems count how many standard lengths weigh a fixed mass, so a higher number means a finer yarn: English cotton count Ne counts 840-yard hanks per pound, metric count Nm counts kilometers per kilogram, and worsted count counts 560-yard hanks per pound. Direct systems, tex and denier, give mass per fixed length, so a higher number means a coarser yarn. Mills, spinners and retailers still quote whichever system their sector grew up with, which is why the system must always be named alongside the number.
example: A shirting yarn is described as 30s cotton. In Ne that means thirty 840-yard hanks weigh one pound. Converting gives about 19.7 tex, about 177 denier and about Nm 51. A student comparing it with a knitwear yarn sold as Nm 2/48 should first recognize that the second number is metric and describes two plies of Nm 48 singles, resulting in roughly Nm 24 before twist contraction.
caution: A bare number such as 40 is meaningless without its system: 40 Ne is a fine cotton yarn, while 40 tex is a much heavier one. Ply notation also differs between trades and regions, so confirm whether a quoted figure is the singles count or the resultant plied count. Count alone does not describe fiber quality, twist, strength or evenness.
deeper: Definitions give the conversions. Ne equals length in yards divided by 840 times mass in pounds; Nm equals length in meters divided by mass in grams. Because tex is grams per 1,000 meters, Nm equals 1,000 divided by tex, and Ne equals about 590.5 divided by tex; Ne is also Nm divided by about 1.693. For worsted count, the 560-yard hank gives tex of roughly 886 divided by the worsted count. Plied yarns in indirect systems combine reciprocally: two singles of count N give a nominal resultant near N divided by 2, whereas in tex the singles values add. ASTM D2260 tabulates conversion factors and equivalent yarn numbers across numbering systems, consistent with ISO 2947.
origins: Indirect counts grew out of reeling practice: yarn was wound into hanks of a customary length, and a spinner's count recorded how many hanks made up a pound. Different sectors fixed different hank lengths, which is why cotton uses 840 yards and worsted 560 yards. Standardization bodies later framed tex as a common metric replacement and published conversion tables so that traditional counts could be translated rather than abandoned overnight.
